title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control of a Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit
authors: Abigail L. Wessels, M. Garrett Bimstefer, Joseph D. Broz, Alen Senanian, Andrew E. Oriani
abstract: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots (TQDs) are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, but the community has so far lacked access to affordable and flexible high-speed control electronics. SpinQICK, an open-source spin qubit-control package built on the Xilinx Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC), directly addresses this gap by leveraging the high sampling-rate signal generation and advanced digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities of the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) to enable precise time-domain voltage control and readout of semiconductor spin qubits. In this paper, we use spinQICK to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. We also introduce and experimentally verify a novel dynamical decoupling (DD) sequence enabled by the triangular TQD and leverage its unique decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise. These results establish spinQICK as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control and provide a pathway for hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.
summary: This paper introduces spinQICK, an open-source control package built on the RFSoC, to overcome the hardware limitations in controlling semiconductor spin qubits. Using a triangular TQD, the authors demonstrate coherent control and state readout, while also pioneering the use of novel Dynamical Decoupling sequences to precisely characterize electrical noise sources. This establishes the RFSoC platform as a flexible and low-cost tool for advancing solid-state quantum computation research.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the lack of affordable and flexible high-speed classical control electronics necessary for scalable quantum information processing using semiconductor spin qubits.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only qubit using the RFSoC-based spinQICK platform, establishing it as a low-cost control solution.
method: The work involves using high-speed DACs and DSP capabilities of the RFSoC to generate precise time-domain voltage pulses for qubit manipulation, alongside implementing Dynamical Decoupling (DD) sequences for noise characterization.
model_or_system: The physical system is a semiconductor triple-quantum dot (TQD) configured as a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. The control Hamiltonian is governed by exchange interactions ($J_{ij}$) modulated by applied voltages.
key_observables: Coherent exchange oscillations ($J_{23}, J_{13}, J_{12}$), return fidelity decay envelopes from DD sequences, and extracted calibration drift frequencies ($\Omega$).
important_parameters: RFSoC DAC sampling rates (6.88 GSPS), pulse widths ($	au_p = 10 	ext{ ns}$), and noise power spectral densities (e.g., $\approx 40 	ext{ nV}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of specific ansatz functions to fit DD return fidelity data to extract drift parameters, and the simulation ignores excited orbital and valley states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate coherent exchange oscillations for the triangular device, the Hamiltonian evolution comparison between linear and triangular geometries, and plots correlating fitted DD oscillation frequencies with elapsed calibration time.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first introducing the limitations of existing control hardware, then demonstrating basic coherent control on the triangular TQD using spinQICK. It then delves into advanced noise characterization using novel DD sequences (NZM1) and concludes by applying fitting techniques to quantify system drift.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware bottleneck in solid-state quantum computing by validating a commercial, open-source platform (RFSoC) for complex, multi-qubit quantum control experiments.

The parameter Nosc given for each axis is defined as the number of exchange oscillations before the amplitude decays by 1/e. Insets: diagrams showing the normalized amplitude of pulses played on each gate of the triangle device to generate a pulse along the defined symmetric exchange axis. The negative voltages are played using the crosstalk compensation feature present in firmware. FIG. 2. spinQICK DD Implementation: (a) Conven- tional EO qubits have a linear arrangement and control is im- plemented with two exchange couplings, J12 and J23. These two couplings can be used to make a DD sequence which de- couples from quasistatic exchange noise. A triangular EO qubit gives an additional exchange coupling, J13, and can be used to create a DD sequence which decouples from qua- sistatic hyperfine noise, as shown in (c). White and grey arrows represent the EO qubit and hyperfine noise spins, re- spectively. In the Bloch sphere representation, the linear ge- ometry (b) enables rotations about the ˆz and ˆn axes whereas the triangular geometry (d) provides a third ˆm axis.

FIG. 3. NZ1 and NZM1 Experiments: Initialization-dependent decay envelopes for NZ1 and NZM1 where (a-c) and (d-f) give their respective return fidelities for initializations along the ˆx, ˆy, and ˆz axes of the Bloch sphere. Initialization in the |1⟩state is implemented with a [DD]X pre-rotation, where [DD] represents a DD sequence. Initializations along ˆx and ˆy are implemented with pre- and post-rotations H[DD]H and HS†[DD]SH, respectively.
